title: How big is Greenland?
hook: Greenland or DR Congo: which has more land? Slide Greenland south and compare.

knows: what a world map looks like

misconception: The sizes of countries on a world map are their real sizes.
objective: The learner can explain that a flat map must distort, that Mercator inflates area away from the equator, and that Greenland is about the size of DR Congo.

claims.text: Greenland's area is about 2.17 million km².
claims.source: CIA World Factbook, Greenland: total area 2,166,086 km². The lesson's own 1:110m data gives about 2.19M km² on a sphere of radius 6,371 km. Fact-check 2026-10-12: Factbook figure confirmed (2021/2022 archives); lesson data recomputed as 2,189,757 km2 (+1.1%).

claims.text: DR Congo's area is about 2.34 million km².
claims.source: CIA World Factbook, Congo, Democratic Republic of the: total area 2,344,858 km². Lesson data gives about 2.33M km². Fact-check 2026-10-12: Factbook figure confirmed; lesson data recomputed as 2,333,678 km2 (-0.5%).

claims.text: On the Mercator map in this lesson, Greenland at its real position is drawn about 15 times the area of DR Congo.
claims.source: v2: map extent reaches about 85.6°N (bottom 61.6°S), so Greenland is drawn whole (bounds y 18.8–98.9 inside 0–236). Projected path areas with d3-geo geoMercator on the lesson data: ratio 15.39 at the real position. v3 re-measured by the builder (scratch script): 15.39, rounded to 15 in the question; the stage readout at the start now uses the same unmoved shape (15.4×) instead of the shape rotated to exactly 73°N (15.0×). The question text is computed from the same map, so they cannot disagree. Needs the fact-checker's re-check. | v5 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): The Mercator map is now 200 px tall with the equator at y 160 (about 86°N to 40°S; was 236 px, 85.6°N to 61.6°S) so it fits beside the reveal on a phone. Greenland is still drawn whole and the question number is computed from the same map, so 15.4x should be unchanged (the r8-style tool run showed 'Seen: Mercator 15.4x at 73°N'), but the ratio has not been re-measured in a script. Reopened; needs a fresh check.

claims.text: Mercator stretches areas more the farther they are from the equator (by about 1/cos²(latitude)).
claims.source: Snyder (1987), Map Projections: A Working Manual, USGS PP 1395, Mercator scale factor k = sec φ, so area factor sec² φ. At 73°, sec² ≈ 11.7. Fact-check 2026-10-12: sec^2(73)=11.70 confirmed; the lesson's own readout 10.73x is still more than ten. v4: the reveal no longer quotes 'more than ten times'; it quotes the stage's own recorded ratios (Seen line) and states only the direction of the stretch. | FC pass 26 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED on derivation (Snyder not opened). Own d3-geo run with the lesson's geoMercator: projected area / true area of a small cell, relative to the equator, is 1.136, 1.717, 4.061, 12.04, 34.88 at 20, 40, 60, 73, 80°, matching 1/cos² of the cell centre to 3 decimals. The reveal states only the direction ("more the farther from the equator"), which holds.

claims.text: Mercator preserves angles, so a line of constant compass bearing is straight on the map.
claims.source: Snyder (1987), ch. 7: Mercator is conformal; rhumb lines are straight lines.

claims.text: Equal Earth is an equal-area projection.
claims.source: Šavrič, Patterson & Jenny (2018), The Equal Earth map projection, IJGIS 33(3).

claims.text: No flat map can preserve both angles and areas everywhere.
claims.source: Gauss's Theorema Egregium (1827): a sphere cannot be mapped to a plane isometrically; a map that is both conformal and equal-area would be an isometry. Snyder (1987), ch. 1.
Unrecorded; found in reveal text. Needs a source (Mercator 1569 world map for navigation).

claims.text: Greenland never changed as you slid it: sliding is a rigid rotation on the sphere that keeps its true area.
claims.source: Unrecorded; reveal text and Demo.tsx comment. Kit moveToLatitude rotates vertices on the sphere. Fact-checker's run on 2026-10-12 found geoArea unchanged to the km2 at targets 0-73N (artifacts/scratch/mercator-greenland-check.mjs), but the fact-checker added this claim and may not verify it.

claims.text: On the real Earth Greenland is about the size of DR Congo (Congo slightly bigger).
claims.source: Unrecorded as its own claim; this is the predict answer and the objective. Follows from c1 and c2 (ratio 0.94 in the lesson data, 0.92 by Factbook areas).

claims.text: A line of one constant compass bearing (a rhumb line) is straight on Mercator and drawn bent on an equal-area map such as Equal Earth.
claims.source: Demo.tsx RHUMB: points with longitude linear in the Mercator ordinate ln tan(45° + lat/2), from 50°W 45°S to 50°E 62°N, 121 samples; by construction a straight segment on Mercator (Snyder 1987, USGS PP 1395, Mercator: rhumb lines are straight). The same points drawn by geoEqualEarth form a curve because Equal Earth's y is not proportional to the Mercator ordinate. Not checked outside the page. | FC pass 26 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED (advisory below). Construction: longitude linear in ln tan(45° + lat/2) is the definition of a rhumb line on Mercator; per-sample great-circle bearings stay 37.2-37.9° (one bearing up to the chord effect). Own d3-geo run on the lesson projections: rendered Mercator path deviates from its chord by at most 0.001 px (straight); on Equal Earth the same points bow 2.8 px off the chord of a 137 px line, so it is bent. Advisory, not a dispute: a 2.8 px (2%) bow on a dashed line may not read as "bent" on a phone; QA or a learner review should confirm it is visible. | v5 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): The orange line still runs from 50°W 45°S to 50°E 62°N, but the shorter Mercator map (bottom about 40°S) now clips its southern end; the equal-area map is now fitted to 320x158 (no empty band) and shows the whole line. The straight/bent behaviour should be re-checked on the new frames. Reopened; needs a fresh check.

recall.question: On a Mercator map, which looks most inflated compared with its real size?
recall.why: Mercator stretches area by about 1/cos²(latitude), so the farther from the equator, the bigger it looks.
